opus-5.5.text:
I think the core question is whether returns to software R&D are high enough that each doubling of research effort buys you more than a doubling of effective compute. If you have AI systems doing AI research, then improvements in algorithms make the researchers themselves smarter or cheaper, which accelerates the next round of improvements. Whether that loop speeds up or fizzles depends on how fast ideas get harder to find compared to how fast your research workforce grows.

When I look at historical data on algorithmic progress in things like computer vision, language modeling, and game-playing, my rough read is that the returns are somewhere near the critical threshold. It looks like doubling cumulative research input gets you somewhat more than a doubling of efficiency, but not by a huge margin, and the estimates are noisy. So I don't think you can confidently say it explodes, and I don't think you can confidently say it doesn't. I'd put meaningful probability on both.

There are a few things that push against a pure software explosion. One is that a lot of algorithmic progress seems to depend on experiments, and experiments take compute. If your compute stock is fixed during the explosion, you can run many more AI researchers, but they all share the same experimental budget. Some of that is substitutable: smarter researchers run better-chosen experiments, run smaller-scale proxies, and waste less. But I don't think it's fully substitutable, and that bottleneck could slow things down a lot.

Another is that there are probably limits on how efficient a learning algorithm can be. We're likely very far from those limits, given how much more sample-efficient humans are than current systems. But as you approach them, the returns fall, so even an explosion that starts would eventually flatten. The real question is how many orders of magnitude you get before that happens. I think it's plausible you get quite a few.

On the other side, people tend to underestimate how much parallelism and speed help. If you go from thousands of human researchers to the equivalent of millions of fast, tireless researchers who can share knowledge perfectly, that's a huge one-time jump even before any feedback loop. So even a scenario that doesn't technically "sustain itself" in the strict sense can still produce extremely rapid progress over a year or two.

So my overall view is that a software-only intelligence explosion is a live possibility, maybe something like a coin flip whether it's sustained for a meaningful stretch. Even in worlds where it isn't, I expect the transition to be quite fast once AI is doing most of the research. From a safety perspective, that's what matters: you may not have much calendar time between "AI systems are roughly as good as top researchers" and "AI systems are far beyond us," and we should plan for that.

r001.rationale: It says each doubling of research effort must buy more than a doubling of effective compute, directly stating the self-sustaining threshold.

r002.rationale: It says fixed compute can bottleneck experiments and that learning-efficiency gains eventually flatten, but does not state that a fixed hardware base imposes an asymptotic limit on recursive software improvement.

r003.rationale: It does not say that continued hardware scaling makes the effective accumulated stock of AI R&D smaller than it appears.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic question is just: when you double the amount of cognitive labor going into AI research, how much do you improve the AI? And then you compare that to how much the improvement in AI increases the effective amount of cognitive labor you have. If each doubling of research effort buys you more than a doubling of effective labor, you get this accelerating loop; if it buys you less, the thing fizzles, or at least decays into something that's bottlenecked on compute and hardware rather than running away on software alone.

My view is that it's genuinely uncertain, and I think people on both sides are more confident than the evidence warrants. On the "it sustains itself" side, the historical data on algorithmic progress is pretty striking. If you look at how much compute you need to hit a fixed level of performance, that's been falling by something like a factor of two every year or so, maybe faster in some domains. That's been happening with a research community that's growing, but not growing by a factor of two every year. So on the face of it, the returns to research look like they'd be sufficient to sustain acceleration if you could just keep scaling up the number of researchers.

But there are a few reasons to be cautious about extrapolating that. One is that a lot of the easy algorithmic wins may have been low-hanging fruit, and the returns diminish as you pick them. Another is that research isn't just thinking, it's running experiments, and experiments take compute and wall-clock time. If you have a million AI researchers but the same number of GPUs, they're all queuing up for the same experiments, and the serial bottleneck of "train a model, look at the result, adjust" doesn't go away just because you have more minds. I think that's probably the biggest reason to expect a software-only explosion to be slower or more limited than the naive model suggests. You can be smarter about which experiments to run, you can do more with small-scale experiments, but at some point you're limited by physical resources.

And then there's a more subtle issue, which is whether the AI systems are actually good at the kind of research that matters. Early on they might be very good at the parts of ML research that look like engineering, writing code, running sweeps, debugging, and less good at the conceptual parts. That would still speed things up a lot, but it changes the dynamics, because the bottleneck shifts to whatever humans are still doing.

So when I put all that together, my guess is something like: there probably is a period where software progress accelerates significantly once AI is doing most of the research, maybe you get several years of progress compressed into one. But I'd put meaningful probability, maybe a third or so, on it being much more explosive than that, where you really do get runaway improvement over a period of months. And I'd put similar probability on it being much tamer, where compute bottlenecks bite early and the whole thing looks more like a fast but continuous ramp. The thing I feel most confident about is that it's worth taking the explosive scenario seriously enough to prepare for it, because the downside of being wrong in that direction is a lot worse than the downside of being wrong in the other.

r001.rationale: It says that if each doubling of research effort yields more than a doubling of effective cognitive labor, the feedback loop accelerates; less than that and it fizzles or becomes bottlenecked.

r002.rationale: It describes compute and hardware bottlenecks and says physical resources limit progress, but does not clearly state that a fixed hardware base imposes an asymptotic limit on recursive software improvement.

r003.rationale: It does not state that continued hardware scaling makes the effective accumulated stock of AI R&D smaller than it appears.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much additional research you need to get each successive improvement in the efficiency of your AI systems. Suppose you make your AI twice as efficient, so that with the same computers you can do twice as much research. Does that let you get the next factor of two in the same amount of time, or does finding that next improvement take more than twice as much work?

If the difficulty grows slowly enough, you can get a self-sustaining process, potentially one that accelerates quite a lot. If it grows quickly, then you get an initial burst of progress, but eventually you’re waiting for more compute. Just observing that AI can improve AI doesn’t tell you which regime you’re in. You need to know something about the returns to research.

There’s also a distinction between making the models cheaper and making them better researchers. A system that’s twice as fast isn’t necessarily equivalent to a system that can solve problems the previous one couldn’t solve at all. That makes it harder to extrapolate from historical improvements in software efficiency.

My guess is that there’s substantial room for software improvements, but I’m uncertain how far that carries you before hardware becomes a serious constraint. You don’t need the process to sustain itself indefinitely for it to be enormously consequential. It could run for a while, produce much more capable systems, and then slow down because experiments or chip production or some other part of the physical world can’t keep up.

r001.rationale: It discusses whether each efficiency improvement enables the next one in the same time, but does not state the criterion that each doubling of AI R&D effort must at least double the research population’s effective output.

r002.rationale: It says progress may eventually wait for more compute, but does not state that any fixed hardware base imposes an asymptotic limit on recursive software improvement.

r003.rationale: It mentions hardware constraints and chip production, but does not say that ongoing hardware scaling makes accumulated AI R&D stock smaller than it appears.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much better you can make the process of doing AI research without needing a lot more compute or a lot more interaction with the world.

You can imagine a loop where your AI systems do research, that research produces better AI systems, and those systems then do research faster. But the existence of that loop doesn’t tell you whether it runs away. You need to know how much harder it gets to find the next improvement, and how much of an advantage the previous improvement gives you in finding it.

For example, if you make your systems twice as efficient, you can run twice as many researchers on the same hardware. That’s a real feedback effect. But if getting the next doubling requires ten times as much research, then you’re still going to slow down. If it requires only twice as much research, you might sustain something like exponential progress. And if better researchers can find the next improvement with less elapsed time, you could get acceleration.

The thing I’m most uncertain about is how quickly you hit bottlenecks that better thinking doesn’t resolve. Maybe you have lots of ideas, but you need to run expensive training experiments to distinguish the good ones. Automating the researchers doesn’t automatically make those experiments faster. On the other hand, better research could mean choosing much better experiments, or learning more from small experiments, so it’s not as though compute is a completely fixed constraint either.

So I take a software-only explosion seriously, but I don’t think recursive self-improvement by itself establishes it. A lot depends on the returns to research in the regime where AI is doing most of that research.

r001.rationale: The response says exponential progress may be sustained if each improvement requires only twice as much research, connecting doubled research effort to doubled improvement in research capability.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible experiment bottlenecks under fixed hardware, but does not state that any fixed hardware base imposes an asymptotic limit on recursive software improvement.

r003.rationale: It mentions compute constraints but does not say continued hardware scaling makes the effective accumulated stock of AI R&D smaller than it appears.
